mcqs.question: How does ARC decide when to deallocate an object, and how does that differ from a tracing garbage collector?
options: It runs a periodic scan for unreachable objects, similar to a tracing garbage collector
It deallocates immediately and synchronously when the object's reference count reaches zero, with no periodic scan or pause
It waits until memory pressure is detected, then deallocates all objects with zero external references
It relies on the developer manually calling a release function at the end of an object's use
mcqs.explanation: ARC inserts retain/release calls at compile time, so deallocation happens deterministically the instant the count hits zero — no periodic sweep, no pause, unlike a tracing garbage collector. Deallocation is automatic, not manual, and doesn't wait for memory pressure.

mcqs.question: You're writing a back-reference where you're not fully certain the referenced object always outlives this one. Which reference type should you default to?
options: weak, since it safely becomes nil rather than crashing if the referent deallocates first
strong, since it guarantees the reference stays valid
unowned, since it has no memory overhead
Either weak or unowned — they behave identically for this case
mcqs.explanation: weak is the safer default when the lifetime relationship isn't guaranteed — it becomes nil gracefully instead of crashing. unowned assumes the referent is guaranteed to outlive the reference; getting that assumption wrong crashes the app on access, which is a much worse failure mode than a nil check.

mcqs.question: A network client stores a completion closure for retry purposes, and the closure captures self strongly to update a property. What's the risk, and what's the fix?
options: No risk — closures never retain self unless explicitly told to
The risk is a data race, fixed by dispatching the closure to a serial queue
self and the stored closure can keep each other alive indefinitely; fix with a [weak self] capture list
The risk is a crash on the next network call, fixed by making the closure @escaping
mcqs.explanation: Closures capture referenced variables strongly by default, and if the closure is stored somewhere that outlives the current call (a retry queue), self and the closure can form a cycle. [weak self] breaks the strong capture. Marking a closure @escaping doesn't fix a cycle — it's often part of what enables one, since it means the closure is stored past the current scope.

mcqs.question: You suspect a view controller is leaking after being dismissed. What's the correct workflow with Instruments' memory graph debugger?
options: Check memory graph before presenting the screen, since leaks only show up on first load
Run the app in release mode only, since the memory graph doesn't work in debug builds
Check the app's total memory footprint in Activity Monitor; the memory graph can't isolate individual leaked objects
Navigate to the screen, dismiss it, then check whether an instance of that view controller still appears as live in the memory graph
mcqs.explanation: The workflow specifically checks for the absence of an object after it should have been deallocated — if an instance still shows as live after dismissal, something unexpected is retaining it, and the graph shows exactly which reference. It works in debug builds and is precisely built to isolate individual object references, not just aggregate memory.

mcqs.question: A Child class declares unowned let parent: Parent, assuming the parent always outlives the child. In production, the app crashes intermittently when accessing parent. What's the most likely cause?
options: unowned references are inherently unstable and should never be used in production code
The child is being retained elsewhere (a cache, an async callback) and accessed after the parent has already deallocated, violating the lifetime assumption unowned depends on
The parent's deinit is being called twice due to a compiler bug
unowned references require explicit synchronization on a background queue
mcqs.explanation: unowned only crashes when the lifetime assumption is actually violated — some other strong reference is keeping the child alive past the parent's deallocation. unowned is a valid, widely-used tool when the assumption genuinely holds; the fix here is switching to weak, not avoiding unowned entirely.

mcqs.question: A screen registers a NotificationCenter observer closure that captures self strongly, and the screen is presented and dismissed many times over a long session. What's the resulting memory pattern?
options: Memory usage stays flat, since NotificationCenter observers are automatically weak
A single large leak appears immediately on first presentation and never grows further
One leaked instance accumulates per presentation-dismissal cycle, causing memory to grow slowly over the session
The app crashes on the second presentation of the screen
mcqs.explanation: Each presentation-dismissal cycle that doesn't clean up the observer leaves one more instance kept alive by the closure's strong self capture, so memory grows incrementally rather than in one jump. NotificationCenter closures are not automatically weak — the capture list has to be set explicitly.
